newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai stocks leap higher, minister confident.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai stocks leap higher, minister confident.

text.p: Thai stocks ended the week with a bang, the baht stabilised and a financial minister said the worst was over for the beleaguered economy although the troubled finance sector would make a slow recovery.

Although some signs of profit-taking began to set in on the Thai stock exchange, the market still ended on Friday more than six percent higher in extremely brisk trade worth 16.5 billion baht ($578.9 million).
Friday's close brings the market's gains up to 130 points in the three days since the government made a shock decision to float the baht.
The baht continued to move in a narrow range against the dollar as some commercial demand for dollars emerged despite the higher baht rates.

Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee said on Friday he expects good times ahead as the finance sector stabilises and the economy improves following the baht float and recent tough financial measures.
"I hope the worst is over," Narongchai told a group of foreign journalists.
But there were still hurdles to overcome, he said.
"For the rest of the year we will see slow recovery in the finance sector. We will have a lesser number but stronger finance companies in the next two to three months," Narongchai said.
Many hope the bitter medicine administered by the Thai government to the economy will allow it to recover.
But both analysts and officials warn it will take time before the economy, mired in its worst slump for more than a decade, can be given a clean bill of health.
Thai stock exchange officials on Friday also announced a widening of the daily stock price trading limit to 30 percent from 10 percent, effective on August 1.
During the recent bourse rally, many major stocks jumped their 10 percent upper daily limit within the first few hours of trade and orders could not be completed.

Since the wider limit was not yet in place on Friday, many foreign investors continued their recent practice of placing buy orders up to the 10 percent limit for almost any blue chip that was available, analysts and traders said.
"Everyone's afraid to be left behind. They're just placing orders for buying up to the 10 percent limit," said George Morgan, country manager at ABN Amro Hoare Govett.
Prices on the no-limits foreign board of shares have rocketed 200-300 percent to levels not seen since July 1995.
"It shows that everyone agrees that you buy after a devaluation and not before. There has been a frantic scramble for stock," said Ian Mclennan, head of research at SBC Warburg.
In the offshore foreign exchange market, business was muted as the baht stabilised near levels reached after losing nearly 20 percent of its value on news of the managed float on Wednesday.
Traders said they would remain firmly on the sidelines after being badly burned by measures taken by the Thai authorities to stem speculation against the baht in the last few weeks.
"I'm not interested at the moment. I'll want to let it all settle down before I go back in," the head of trading at a European bank said.

Since the baht last came under attack in May, coordinated central bank intervention, the imposition of capital controls and a sharp rise in interest rates have made speculators wary of the Thai currency -- despite Wednesday's de facto devaluation.
On Friday, the Bank of Thailand announced a new daily reference rate for the currency of 28.189 to the dollar, slightly weaker than Thursday's 27.383.

In the domestic market the baht was trading late at around 28.50/29.00 to the dollar compared to 28.25/28.65 late on Thursday. Offshore, the currency was quoted around 28.70/29.00 versus 29.00/29.50 late on Thursday.
Dealers and investors were still digesting the change from a 13-year-old system which had pegged the baht to a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.
The new reference rate is a weighted average of the previous day's trading levels. ($ = 28.5 baht)
